The Greek features on SPXW same-day options

    Seller, for the charts and bucket tables of section 1

    1. Delta ÷ gamma and delta² ÷ gamma

    A straddle that starts with no delta and sees the index move x points ends with a delta of about gamma × x. So delta ÷ gamma is about x, a distance in index points, and delta² ÷ (2 gamma) is the gain that a hedge made now would lock in for the holder. For the seller it is the loss. Divide it by the theta earned over the window and the result is a realised-over-implied ratio of the end point: above 1 the window lost, below 1 it earned. All of these are known only when the window ends. They explain a result and predict nothing.

    Which measure explains which seller

    Rank correlation of each measure with the seller's result over the same window. A figure nearer −1 explains more.

    2. Charm and colour: how much of the hedging is caused by the clock

    Each one-minute change in the pair's delta is taken apart by repricing with one input changed at a time: the forward (the market), one minute off the clock (charm), then implied volatility. The three parts add up to the whole change. The shares are of the sizes of the parts, added over all minutes. Two positions: a new at-the-money straddle every 30 minutes, and the 9:35 straddle held to 15:35.

    By distance from the strike, for the straddle held all day

    Distance is in implied moves: one implied move is one standard deviation of the index's move in the time left.

    Colour: where the clock gives gamma and where it takes it

    For every one-minute step of both positions: did the minute passing raise the pair's gamma or lower it?

    A window that ends more than one implied move from its strike

    The seller hedged every minute at the mid, by where the 30-minute window ended.

    3. Implied volatility against the index

    The Black delta assumes implied volatility stays where it is when the index moves. The slope is the one-minute change in the implied volatility of the held strike per unit of log return of the forward. A slope of −1 means a 1% rise takes one volatility point off.
